questions.q: What is the trust boundary of an HTTP API?
questions.explain: Every value from outside is untrusted until a schema has checked it. Validate at the boundary, once, and the services behind it can rely on clean, typed data.
options: The line between the service and the store
The place where outside data (route parameters, query string, headers, body) comes into your program
The firewall in front of the server
The list of users who may log in

questions.q: Which of these does not need a schema check at the boundary of the Task API?
questions.explain: Route parameters, query strings, headers and bodies come from the client, so they are untrusted. A value your own code computes did not cross the boundary.
options: The createdAt date the service computes with its own clock

questions.q: What is the difference between parse and safeParse?
questions.explain: Both run the same rules. Use parse when a failure should become an error (a 400 in a route), and safeParse when you want to look at the issues yourself.
options: safeParse is slower but checks more rules
parse throws a SchemaError on bad input; safeParse returns { success, data } or { success, issues }
parse only checks types; safeParse also checks lengths

questions.q: A schema issue has a code, a path and a message. Which is meant for your program to react to?
questions.explain: The code is stable for programs, the message is text for people, and the path says which field it is about.
options: None: issues are only for people

questions.q: An issue has path: ["tags", 1]. What does it point at?
questions.explain: A path lists the keys and indexes from the top of the value down to the field. Array indexes start at 0, so 1 is the second item.
options: The second tag (index 1 of the tags array)

questions.q: What does schema.safeParse(value, { abortEarly: true }) do?
questions.explain: Normally all issues are reported at once, which is what a form wants. When you only need to know "valid or not", abortEarly saves work.
options: Stops the program when the value is invalid
Stops at the first problem instead of collecting all of them
Skips the checks and returns the value
Only checks the first field of the object

questions.q: Where should you use schema.coerce.number() instead of schema.number()?
questions.explain: A JSON body has real numbers and booleans. Coercing there would accept "1" where the client should have sent 1, and hide the client's mistake.
options: Everywhere, because it accepts more input
For input that really arrives as text: query strings, route parameters, headers, environment variables

questions.q: Why use schema.coerce.boolean() for ?done=false instead of Boolean(ctx.query.done)?
questions.explain: Any non-empty string is truthy. The coercing schema knows the words: "true", "1", "yes", "on" become true, "false" becomes false.
options: Boolean("false") is true; the schema turns "false" into false and refuses text it does not understand

questions.q: A schema is schema.string().max(200).transform((text) => text.split(",")). What does Infer<typeof TagList> give?
questions.explain: The schema accepts a string, but its output type follows whatever the transform function returns: an array of strings.

questions.q: When does a .transform(fn) function run?
questions.explain: The transform receives a value that is already valid. For 42, which is not a string, the transform never runs and the parse fails.
options: Before the checks, on the raw input
Only after the checks before it have passed

questions.q: You need a rule that compares two fields of an object (reminder date not after due date). How do you write it?
questions.explain: A field-level rule only sees its own field. .transform() and .refine() exist as methods on string and number schemas; for objects, use the wrapper functions schema.refine(inner, check, message) and schema.transform(inner, fn).
options: Add .refine() to one of the two string fields
Check it in every route by hand
It cannot be done with a schema

questions.q: Should the schema check "does a task with this title already exist?" in a refine?
questions.explain: A schema checks the value itself, nothing else. Rules that need stored data belong in the service, which knows the store and throws the right error (409).
options: Yes, refinements are for every rule
No: refinements should be synchronous and pure; a check that needs the database belongs in the service, which throws ConflictError
No, it belongs in the router

questions.q: Why does comparing value.remindOn <= value.dueOn as strings work for YYYY-MM-DD dates?
questions.explain: Year first, then month, then day, each with a fixed number of digits: comparing character by character gives the same order as comparing the dates. That is not true for DD/MM/YYYY.
options: JavaScript converts date strings to dates automatically
In YYYY-MM-DD form, the text sorts in the same order as the dates themselves
It does not work; you must use Date.parse
Because both strings have the same length

questions.q: Why does the lesson write the PATCH update schema by hand, without defaults?
questions.explain: Defaults describe creating a task. An update should change only the fields the client sent, so its schema lists the changeable fields, all optional, with no defaults.
options: An update must not invent values: a default like priority: "normal" could reset a stored high priority the client never mentioned

questions.q: An object schema gets a body with an extra key id. What is the difference between the default behaviour and .strict()?
questions.explain: Stripping is already safe: the extra key never reaches your code. .strict() goes further, so a client that sends a field you do not accept learns about its mistake.
options: By default the key is stripped (dropped from the result); .strict() rejects the body with an issue
By default the body is rejected; .strict() strips the key

questions.q: What is mass assignment?
questions.explain: The defence is an explicit schema that lists exactly the changeable fields (strict or stripping), and code that copies only those fields. Never write { ...task, ...body }.
options: Creating many tasks in one request
Copying request fields blindly onto a stored object, so a client can add "ownerId" or "role": "admin" and take over data or rights
Assigning the same value to many variables

questions.q: Which update code is safe?
questions.explain: Parse first, then copy each known field. Only the listed fields can change, and a field the client did not send keeps its stored value. as StoredTask only hides the problem from TypeScript.
options: const changes = UpdateTaskSchema.parse(body); return { ...task, title: changes.title ?? task.title, done: changes.done ?? task.done };

questions.q: Why send every task through a TaskResponse schema before it leaves the server?
questions.explain: Object schemas strip unknown keys, so parsing the stored object keeps only the fields you chose to publish, including after someone adds new internal fields next year.
options: To make the JSON smaller by removing spaces
It is an allow-list: only the listed fields go out, so internal fields like ownerId or a password hash never leak
Because clients cannot read objects that were not parsed
To add default values for the client

questions.q: A stored task is missing its priority, and TaskResponse.parse(task) fails in a route. What status is right?
questions.explain: The client sent nothing wrong. A response that does not match its schema means the server has a bug, and the response schema caught it before the client saw bad data.
options: 404, because the priority was not found
500: it is a bug in your own code, not a client mistake, so let it fail and fix the bug

questions.q: Why run assertDepthWithinLimit and assertSizeWithinLimit before the schema?
questions.explain: A schema walks the whole value. The structural guards are cheap checks that refuse absurd input before any expensive work starts.
options: A hostile client can send JSON built to make the schema's walk expensive (thousands of levels deep, megabytes in one field); the guards stop cheaply as soon as a limit is passed
They turn the body into a string

questions.q: @zudojs/validation also has a complete Zod-based schema system. What does the course advise?
questions.explain: The two systems do not share schemas. Mixing them means writing every rule twice.
options: Use both systems for every value, to be safe
Pick one schema system per project; the course uses @zudojs/schema and only borrows the guards
Use Zod for bodies and @zudojs/schema for responses

questions.explain: "2" becomes the number 2, "false" the boolean false, and missing values get their defaults: page 1, 20 per page.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The coercing schema knows the words: "yes" and "1" mean true, "false" means false. Plain Boolean("false") is true, because every non-empty string is truthy.

questions.explain: An empty page= is refused instead of quietly becoming 0. "7.5" is a number, but not a whole one.

limit: Expected integer, received 7.5
page: Cannot coerce string to number

questions.q: The client sent ?page=1&page=2. What does this print?
questions.explain: A repeated query key arrives as an array of strings, which cannot become one number, so the schema refuses it.
options: false Cannot coerce array to number
true Cannot coerce array to number

questions.q: A JSON body sends "1" where a number was expected. What does this print?
questions.explain: schema.number() refuses the string, so the client learns it sent the wrong type. That is what you want for JSON bodies; coerce is for input that can only be text.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The transform splits, trims, lower-cases and drops the empty piece between the two commas. For 42 the string check fails first, so the transform never runs.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: trim() and toLowerCase() are small built-in transformations. After trimming, " " is empty, so min(1) refuses it instead of matching every task.

questions.explain: The rule belongs to the whole object, so its issue has an empty path. Your own rules report the code custom with your message.
options:
true

true

questions.explain: .strict() rejects every key the schema does not list, and names each one, so the client learns exactly what it sent wrong.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: By default an object schema strips unknown keys: they disappear from the result, so they can never be copied onto a stored task.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The response schema is an allow-list: the internal fields are dropped, and only the published ones leave the server.
options: { id: 7, title: 'Buy milk', done: false, ownerId: 42, internalNotes: 'flagged' }
{ id: 7, title: 'Buy milk', done: false, ownerId: 42 }

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The response schema caught a stored task with a missing field, a bug in your own code, before it was sent. In a route, let that become a 500 and fix the bug.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: parse throws a SchemaError, which carries status 400. That is why @zudojs/http answers a failed parse in a route with a 400 by itself.
options: TypeError 400 id must be at least 1

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An array nested 500 levels deep passes the limit of 10, so the guard stops it before any schema has to walk it. A normal task is only a few levels deep.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 50 000 characters is far over the 16 384-byte limit (the estimate counts two bytes per character). The error carries 413, the status for a body that is too large.

questions.q: Finish fieldErrors: turn the issues into an object with one message per field. The key is issue.path.join("."), or "(body)" when the path is empty, and only the first message for a field is kept. The program should print { title: 'String must be at least 3 characters', 'tags.1': 'Expected string, received number' }.
questions.explain: ??= only sets the key when it has no message yet, so the first problem per field wins. A web form can show each message next to its input.
questions.expected: { title: 'String must be at least 3 characters', 'tags.1': 'Expected string, received number' }

questions.q: Write ListTasksQuery with page (a whole number, at least 1, default 1) and limit (a whole number from 1 to 50, default 20). Both arrive as query strings, so coerce them. The program should print 2 10, 1 20 and false.
questions.explain: schema.coerce.number() turns the text into a number, .int().min().max() check it, and .default() fills in a missing value. A limit of 500 is refused, so one request cannot ask for everything.

questions.q: Add a .transform to TagList that splits the text on commas, trims and lower-cases each tag, and drops empty tags. The program should print [ 'home', 'urgent', 'errands' ].
questions.explain: The transform runs after the string checks pass, and its return value (an array) becomes the schema's output.

questions.q: Finish isRealDate: build the date with new Date(Date.UTC(year, month - 1, day)) and return true only when its toISOString().slice(0, 10) equals the text (so 30 February, which rolls over to March, is refused). The program should print true false false.
questions.explain: JavaScript rolls impossible dates over: 30 February becomes 2 March, and month 13 becomes next January. Comparing the result with the original text catches that. A refinement returns true when the value is fine.

questions.q: Wrap the object with schema.refine so it fails with the message Passwords do not match when password and confirm differ. The program should print true and then Passwords do not match.
questions.explain: A rule that compares two fields belongs on the object: schema.refine(inner, check, message). The check is synchronous and pure; it only looks at the value.

questions.q: Make UpdateTask refuse unknown keys, so a client cannot send ownerId. The program should print true and then [ 'Unknown key: ownerId' ].
questions.explain: Without .strict(), ownerId would be quietly stripped (safe, but silent). .strict() rejects it, so the client learns about its mistake.

questions.q: Finish applyChanges the safe way: copy only title and done, each with ?? so a field the client did not send keeps its stored value. Never spread changes. The program should print { id: 1, ownerId: 7, title: 'Buy milk', done: true }.
questions.explain: Copying each known field means ownerId can never change (no mass assignment), and ?? task.title keeps the stored title when the change is undefined. { ...task, ...changes } would both lose the title and hand the task to user 1.
questions.expected: { id: 1, ownerId: 7, title: 'Buy milk', done: true }

questions.q: Finish sentOnly: return a copy of changes without the keys whose value is undefined. Use Object.entries, filter and Object.fromEntries. The program should print { done: true } and then { id: 1, title: 'Buy milk', done: true }.
questions.explain: A key set to undefined still overwrites when you spread it. Dropping those keys first keeps the stored title. Only do this with parsed changes, never with a raw body.
questions.expected:
{ done: true }
{ id: 1, title: 'Buy milk', done: true }

questions.q: Write TaskResponse, an object schema with exactly id (number), title (string, at most 100) and done (boolean). Parsing the stored user task must drop the internal fields. The program should print { id: 7, title: 'Buy milk', done: false }.
questions.explain: Object schemas strip unknown keys, so a response schema is an allow-list: ownerId and passwordHash never leave the server, even if someone adds more internal fields later.

questions.q: Finish checkBody: run assertDepthWithinLimit(body, 10) and assertSizeWithinLimit(body, 16384). Return "ok" when both pass, 400 when the error's name is SerializationDepthError (a too-deep body is the client's mistake), and the error's statusCode otherwise. The program should print ok 400 413.
questions.explain: The guards are cheap and stop as soon as a limit is passed, before any schema walks the body. A too-deep body and a too-large body are both the client's fault, so they get 4xx answers.
